name: Double-Entry Bookkeeping
intent: Record every movement of money as an immutable journal entry whose debits equal its credits, derive balances from the entries, and fix mistakes with new reversing entries, so the books can always prove that they balance.
scenario: A payment platform holds four accounts: cash at the bank, customer wallets, money owed to merchants, and fee revenue. It takes a 100.00 card payment with a 3.00 fee, then refunds, pays out and corrects entries. Next to it, a second design keeps a single balance number per account and updates it in place.
problem: When a balance is a number that code reads, changes and writes back, money can disappear without a trace. Two payments that arrive together both read the same old balance and one write overwrites the other, a bug that adds 50 to the wrong account leaves no record that the 50 ever moved, and an engineer who edits a balance to fix it makes the audit trail worse. Nothing in the data says whether the numbers are right, so finding a cent that is missing means comparing against outside systems and guessing.

howItWorks.title: Every movement is an entry with two sides
howItWorks.text: Money never appears or vanishes: it moves from somewhere to somewhere. A journal entry lists the accounts it touches, with an amount on the debit side or the credit side of each. A card payment of 100.00 with a 3.00 fee debits cash at the bank by 100.00 and credits merchant payable by 97.00 and fee revenue by 3.00. Debits and credits are only the two sides of the ledger: assets and expenses normally grow with debits, liabilities, equity and revenue normally grow with credits.

howItWorks.title: An entry must balance, or it is rejected
howItWorks.text: The one rule the system enforces: the sum of debits equals the sum of credits, in the same currency, before the entry is stored. In code it is a check on the signed amounts adding up to zero. An entry with 50.00 in and 49.00 out is refused with the difference named, instead of being stored and discovered during a month-end close. The check lives in the one place all writes pass through.

howItWorks.title: Entries are immutable, and balances are derived
howItWorks.text: An entry is only ever appended: it is never updated or deleted. The balance of an account is the sum of its lines, which can be computed on demand, or kept as a cache that is rebuilt from the journal when in doubt. Two payments that arrive at the same moment simply append two entries, and no write overwrites another. The history answers what happened, when, and in what order.

howItWorks.title: Correct with a reversal, never an edit
howItWorks.text: A mistake is fixed by appending a new entry that reverses the wrong one (the same lines with debits and credits swapped), then, if needed, a correct entry. The wrong entry stays in the journal, linked to its reversal, so an auditor can see both the error and the fix. A refund is the same idea: a new entry in the opposite direction, not a deletion of the payment.

howItWorks.title: The trial balance proves the books
howItWorks.text: Add up every debit and every credit across all accounts: the totals must be equal, so the difference is zero. If it is not zero, an entry was stored without being checked, or a line was lost. Because balanced entries are the only way in, the trial balance is a cheap check that can run every night. It cannot prove that the right accounts were used or that the amounts are true, and a whole balanced entry posted twice or never posted passes it too: it proves only that what is stored balances. Reconciliation with the bank covers the rest.

pros: A complete, ordered audit trail: every balance can be explained by the entries behind it
Unbalanced writes are rejected at the door, and the trial balance detects lost lines
Concurrent operations append entries instead of overwriting a balance
Corrections keep the original mistake visible, which auditors and regulators expect
cons: More rows and more concepts than one balance column: every operation needs its accounts and sides decided up front
Reading a balance means summing entries, so busy accounts need cached or snapshotted balances kept in step
Hot accounts (a single fee account touched by every payment) become a write bottleneck and may need splitting
A reversal for every mistake means the journal grows, and a cancelled operation still leaves two entries
whenToUse: Anything that holds money for others: wallets, marketplaces, payment platforms, payroll, billing
Systems where money moves between several parties and each cent must be accounted for
Anywhere an auditor, a regulator or a partner bank may ask how a balance came to be
whenNotToUse: Counters that are not money (likes, stock levels, usage metrics), where a simple counter or an event log is enough
A single-party tally with no obligations to anyone else, such as a personal budget script
Prototypes where nothing real is at stake yet, though the cost of starting with a journal is small
pitfalls: Keeping a balance column as the source of truth and the journal only as a log, so the two drift apart and nobody knows which is right
Editing or deleting an entry to fix a mistake instead of appending a reversal
Allowing a single entry to mix currencies, so the zero-sum check means nothing
Updating a cached balance in the same step as the append without a transaction, so the cache and the journal disagree
Treating a zero trial balance as proof that the amounts are right: it proves only that entries balance
One hot account that every payment updates, which serializes all writes behind a single row

roles.label: Payer
roles.description: Pays by card or tops up a wallet.

roles.label: Payment service
roles.description: Builds entries and posts them to the journal.

roles.label: Journal
roles.description: Append-only list of balanced entries, the source of truth.

roles.label: Accounts
roles.description: Cash, wallets, merchant payable and fee revenue, with balances derived from the journal.

roles.label: Auditor
roles.description: Runs the trial balance and reads the history.

quiz.question: A refund of a 100.00 payment is needed. In a double-entry system, how is it recorded?
options: Delete the payment entry, so the balances return to what they were.
Edit the payment entry and set its amount to zero, keeping its id.
Subtract 100.00 from the merchant's balance column, then log a note.
Append a new entry that moves the money back, leaving the payment in place.
quiz.explanation: Entries are immutable, so history is never rewritten: the refund is a new entry in the opposite direction. Deleting or editing the payment would destroy the audit trail, and changing only a balance column leaves no entry that explains the change.

quiz.question: Two payments to the same merchant are processed at exactly the same moment. Which design can lose one of them?
options: A journal with two appended entries and balances summed from the journal.
A balance column that each request reads, increases and writes back with no check.
A journal whose entries are checked to balance before they are stored.
A trial balance run every night over all the entries in the journal.
quiz.explanation: With read, add, write back, both requests read the same old balance and the later write wins, so one payment vanishes without a trace. Appending entries does not overwrite anything, and the sum of both is correct.

quiz.question: The nightly trial balance shows a difference of zero. What does that prove?
options: That every amount is correct and every payment went to the right account.
That the bank statement matches the ledger, so no reconciliation is needed.
That debits equal credits across the books, so no unbalanced entry or lost line got in.
That no entry was ever reversed, since a reversal would make the total non-zero.
quiz.explanation: The trial balance only checks that debits equal credits. A wrong account or a wrong amount that still balances passes it, and a reversal is itself a balanced entry. Matching against the bank is a separate step, called reconciliation.
